orient: Narrator: Lockwood at first, back at Thrushcross Grange with a cold. After the row of asterisks, his housekeeper Mrs. Dean (Nelly) takes over and tells the story, going back about thirty years. Scholars usually date the arrival she describes to the summer of 1771.

notes.n: A weathercock is a weathervane that turns with every wind. Lockwood swore off company yesterday, and today he is lonely.

notes.g: Social contact; talking and spending time with people.
notes.m: 'Intercourse' just meant dealings or conversation. No sexual meaning.

notes.n: From the old belief that the stars controlled your fortune.
A naval phrase: a ship surrendered by lowering ('striking') its flag.

notes.g: Lockwood's housekeeper at the Grange: the 'fixture' from Chapter II.
notes.n: She grew up around Wuthering Heights and becomes the main storyteller of the novel. Her first name is Ellen, and people call her Nelly.

notes.m: Since 'dinner' was at midday, the evening meal was 'supper'.

notes.g: A real chatterbox; someone who loves to talk about others.
When the lady of this house (the late Mrs. Linton) got married.
Kept me on in his service.

notes.m: A noun here: like an 'exotic' plant brought from abroad.

notes.g: Latin: the natives; the local people.
notes.n: Lockwood's showy Latin, treating the Yorkshire folk like a foreign tribe.

notes.m: To 'let' a house means to rent it out, not to allow.

notes.g: An unknown amount of money; lots of it.

notes.m: 'Near' here means tight-fisted, not close by.

notes.n: Still used in Scotland and the north of England.

notes.g: A few hundred pounds more (in rent).
The daughter of my former master, who is now dead.
notes.n: 'Late' means dead. Her master was Mr. Linton of Thrushcross Grange.

notes.t: Catherine Linton was her maiden name
notes.g: Before marrying, young Mrs. Heathcliff was called Catherine Linton.
notes.n: A 'maiden name' is a woman's surname before marriage. Lockwood is startled because Catherine Linton is the ghost's name from Chapter III. But this is a different, younger Catherine.

notes.g: I looked after her as a child.
notes.m: A 'nurse' here is a nanny or children's maid, not a hospital nurse.

notes.g: The person who lived here before me.
Hareton's aunt was the late Mrs. Linton, young Catherine's mother.
notes.n: Later in this chapter Nelly mentions that Hareton's father is Hindley Earnshaw. So Mrs. Linton was born an Earnshaw: Hindley's sister. Remember the names on the window ledge.

notes.t: one on the mother’s, the other on the father’s side
notes.g: Young Catherine has two cousins: Hareton (through her mother) and her dead husband (through her father).
notes.n: Her father's sister married Heathcliff, so Heathcliff's son was her cousin too. Families marrying cousins was common then, especially in remote places.

notes.g: Nelly's pet name for young Mrs. Heathcliff, whom she raised.
notes.n: Careful: in Nelly's story below, 'Miss Cathy' means a different girl.

notes.g: A different Cathy: Catherine Earnshaw as a little girl.
notes.n: This is the Catherine of the diary in Chapter III, Hindley's sister. Don't mix her up with young Mrs. Heathcliff ('our Miss Cathy' above).

notes.g: As rough as the teeth of a saw.
A very hard, dark rock found in the north of England.
notes.n: Used for road stone because it is so tough.

notes.g: His history is like a cuckoo's.
notes.n: A cuckoo lays its egg in another bird's nest. The cuckoo chick then pushes the other chicks out. Nelly means Heathcliff was an outsider who took over a family that wasn't his.

notes.g: A baby hedge sparrow that has no feathers yet.
notes.n: Dunnocks are a common victim of cuckoos. Hareton is the chick pushed out of his own nest.

notes.g: The local district served by one church; the neighbourhood.
Thin, runny porridge, given to sick people.
A flat shelf beside the fireplace where pots and dishes are kept warm.

notes.t: my mother had nursed Mr. Hindley Earnshaw
notes.g: Nelly's mother had been Hindley's nurse when he was a baby.
notes.n: So Nelly grew up at Wuthering Heights almost as one of the household, though she was a servant's child. She is about Hindley's age.
So the Hindley of Catherine's diary is Hareton's father. 'That was' means 'who was'.

notes.g: Cut grass and dry it in the sun to feed animals in winter.
Late summer, when the grain crops are cut.
Hindley and Catherine's father, who owned Wuthering Heights then.

notes.n: 'Bonny' means handsome or fine, still common in northern England and Scotland.

notes.g: A large port city about sixty miles from the Heights.
notes.n: In the 1770s Liverpool was Britain's busiest port, and a centre of the slave trade, full of sailors and immigrants. Readers have long wondered where Heathcliff came from. The book never says.

notes.g: About 100 km each way, on foot.
notes.n: 120 miles in three days shows how tough the old farmer is.

notes.g: A long stretch; a long way.
Not for anything in the world.
notes.n: The 'three kingdoms' were England, Scotland and Ireland, all ruled by one king.

notes.g: You'll just have to accept it.
notes.n: 'E'en' is short for 'even'.

notes.t: as dark almost as if it came from the devil
notes.g: The child is so dark-skinned he might be the devil's.
notes.n: From the start, Heathcliff's darkness marks him as an outsider. Notice how Nelly calls him 'it'.
He seems to speak a language none of them know.

notes.g: Bring himself to bring; have the nerve to bring.
notes.n: The same dialect verb Joseph used in Chapter II ('faishion').

notes.g: An insulting name: a dark-skinned beggar child.
notes.n: 'Gipsy' is an old, now offensive term for the Romani people, used here as an insult because of his looks.

notes.m: 'Dumb' meant mute, unable to talk, not stupid.

notes.g: That I was sent away forever.
Gave him a name (literally, baptised him).

notes.t: the name of a son who died in childhood
notes.g: The Earnshaws' own dead child had been called Heathcliff.
notes.n: So he is named after a lost son, which may explain some of Mr. Earnshaw's love for him.

notes.g: As both his first name and his family name.
notes.n: He has only the one name, Heathcliff, and no family name of his own.

notes.t: plagued and went on with him
put in a word on his behalf

notes.g: Spoiling him; making a pet of him.
Mr. Earnshaw's wife: Hindley and Catherine's mother.
Someone who treats you cruelly or unjustly.
Someone who wrongfully takes another person's place.
notes.n: As the eldest son, Hindley expected to be first in his father's love and to inherit the farm.

notes.g: Thinking resentfully about something for a long time.
Caught measles, a serious and often deadly childhood disease then.

notes.t: take on me the cares of a woman at once
notes.g: Suddenly do an adult woman's work.
notes.n: Nelly is still a teenager herself.

notes.g: The person who helps and supports him (Mr. Earnshaw).
The local fair, where farmers bought and sold animals and goods.
Became unable to walk properly (of a horse, an injured leg).
Bruised black all the way up.
Hit him on the side of the head.
With extra on top (like interest on a loan).

notes.t: an iron weight used for weighing potatoes and hay
notes.g: A heavy iron weight for a balance scale.
Throw me out of the house.

notes.m: A time word here, not 'in a straight line'.

notes.t: letting his condition plead for him
notes.g: Letting his injuries speak for themselves.

notes.n: An 'interloper' pushes in where he doesn't belong; 'beggarly' means poor and worthless.

notes.g: Coax and flatter someone into giving you things.
Little devil; child of the devil.
A horse's own space in a stable.
A sudden feeling of sickness or faintness.
notes.m: Not a doubt or worry of conscience, its usual sense today.

notes.t: I was deceived completely, as you will hear
notes.g: Nelly hints at what is coming.
notes.n: Storytellers often drop hints like this ('foreshadowing'). Keep it in mind.
